label: thm:main
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $n\ge2$ and assume that
\[
\begin{cases}
1\le q<p<\infty, \qquad& n=2,\\
1\le q<p<\dfrac{n+2}{n-2}, \qquad& n\ge3.
\end{cases}
\]
Then, for every integer $k\ge1$, the equation
\[
\Delta u-\lvertu\rvert^{q-1}u+\lvertu\rvert^{p-1}u=0
\quad\text{in }\mathbb R^n
\]
possesses exactly one radial $k$-node bound state satisfying $u(0)>0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Existence follows from the prescribed-node existence theorem of \cite{MTW1990}. For $n=2$, uniqueness follows from \cite[Theorem~1.1]{CGHY2011}. For $n\ge3$, the cases $q>1$ and $q=1$ follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:main} and \cite{Tang2026}, respectively.

label: lem:nodal-geometry
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:nodal-geometry}
Let $u$ be a nontrivial solution of \eqref{eq:shoot}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $z_1$ is the first zero of $u$, then $\alpha=u(0)>\beta$ and
$u'(r)<0$ for $0<r< z_1$.
\item Between two consecutive zeros of $u$, there is exactly one critical point.
\item If $u$ is a bound state, then after its last zero, there is exactly one critical point; beyond it $u$ is monotone and converges to zero.
\item For a bound state, $E(r)>0$ for all $r>0$.
If
$c_-<c_+$ are consecutive critical points separated by a zero, then
$\lvertu(c_-)\rvert>\lvertu(c_+)\rvert>\beta$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $z_1$ is simple,
\[
 F(\alpha)=E(0)>E(z_1)=\frac12u'(z_1)^2>0.
\]
Thus $\alpha>\beta$, and radial regularity gives
$u''(0)=-f(\alpha)/n<0$.  Suppose that $u'$ has a first zero $c\in(0,z_1)$.
Then $u'<0$ on $(0,c)$, $u'(c)=0$ and $u''(c)\ge0$.  On the other hand,
$F(u(c))=E(c)>E(z_1)>0$, so $u(c)>\beta$ and
$u''(c)=-f(u(c))<0$.  This contradiction proves \textup{(i)}.

Rolle's theorem gives at least one critical point between consecutive zeros.  At any critical point $c$ preceding a later zero $z$, strict energy decay gives
\[
 F(u(c))=E(c)>E(z)=\frac12u'(z)^2>0,
\]
so $\lvertu(c)\rvert>\beta$. By $u''(c)=-f(u(c))$, a critical point with $u>0$ is therefore a strict local maximum, while one with $u<0$ is a strict local minimum.  Two critical points of the same type would force a critical point of the opposite type between them, which is impossible.  This proves \textup{(ii)}.

After the last zero of a bound state, $u$ has fixed sign and tends to zero.  Since $F(u(r))\to0$ and $E$ decreases, $E(r)$ has a limit $L\ge0$.  If $L>0$, then $u'(r)^2=2(E(r)-F(u(r)))$ is bounded away from zero for all large $r$, contradicting $u(r)\to0$.  Hence $L=0$ and $u'(r)\to0$.  The derivative immediately after the last zero points into the fixed-sign half-line, so it must vanish before the solution can return to zero at infinity.  At such a critical point $E(c)>0$, hence $\lvertu(c)\rvert>\beta$, and the same critical-point argument gives uniqueness.  This proves \textup{(iii)}.

Since $E$ is strictly
decreasing and $E(r)\downarrow0$ along the tail,
we obtain $E(r)>0$ for all $r>0$.  Finally, $E(c_+)<E(c_-)$ and $F$ is
strictly increasing as a function of $\lverts\rvert$ on $\lverts\rvert>1$.  Since both
amplitudes exceed $\beta>1$, statement \textup{(iv)} follows.

label: lem:Ppositive
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Ppositive}
Let $u$ be a bound state of \eqref{eq:shoot}.
Then $P(r)>0$ and $P_2(r)>0$ at every positive radius belonging to a finite nodal phase of $u$.
Consequently, $P/r^n$ is strictly decreasing there.  On every subinterval where $\lvertu\rvert\geq1$, one also has $P_1>0$ and hence $\omega'>0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
At any simple zero $z$ of $u$,
\[
 P(z)=P_2(z)=z^n u'(z)^2>0.
\]
At any critical point \(c>0\) such that \(u\) has at least one zero in $(c,\infty)$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:nodal-geometry} gives $|u(c)|>\beta$, and therefore
\[
 P(c)=2c^nF(u(c))>0,
 \qquad
 P_2(c)=\frac{n-2}{n}c^n u(c)f(u(c))>0.
\]
At the origin, $P(0)=P_2(0)=0$.

For  $t>0$, both functions
$h(t)$ and $h_2(t)$ have exactly one positive zero, are negative
below that zero, and positive above it.  Consider first a prezero
half-phase, on which $|u|$ decreases strictly.  The identities
\[
 P'=r^{n-1}h(|u|),\qquad
 P_2'=\frac{r^n|u'|}{n}h_2(|u|)
\]
show that both $P$ and $P_2$ can first increase and then
decrease, but cannot have an interior minimum.
Since they are nonnegative at the preceding endpoint
and strictly positive at the subsequent zero,
both remain strictly positive throughout the interior.

On a postzero half-phase, $uu'>0$, and the energy is strictly
positive by Lemma~\ref{lem:nodal-geometry}.  Consequently,
\[
 P=2r^nE+(n-2)r^{n-1}uu'>0.
\]
Moreover, $|u|$ is now increasing and the parity of $h_2$ yields
\[
 P_2'=-\frac{r^n|u'|}{n}h_2(|u|).
\]
Its derivative has the increase--decrease sign pattern.  Since
$P_2>0$ at both endpoints, it is positive throughout.  This proves
$P,P_2>0$ on every finite phase.  The identity for $(P/r^n)'$ now
implies its strict decrease.  Finally $h_1(u)>0$ for $|u|\ge1$,
so $P_1=P+r^nh_1(u)>0$ and $\omega'>0$ wherever $|u|\ge 1$.

label: lem:Ptail
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Ptail}
Let $u$ be a bound state of \eqref{eq:shoot} and let $c$ be its last critical point.
If $c>0$, then $P(r)>0$ for $r\ge c$.  If $c=0$, then
$P(r)>0$ for $r>0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After reflection if necessary, assume $u>0$, $u'<0$, and $u\to0$ on
$(c,\infty)$.  Then $E(r)\downarrow0$ and $u'(r)\to0$.
For all sufficiently large $r$, one has $0<u(r)<1$ and $f(u)<0$.  Put
\[
 y(r):=-r^{n-1}u'(r)>0.
\]
Since $y'(r)=r^{n-1}f(u(r))<0$ on the small-amplitude tail, $y$ is bounded there.  From
\[
 P(r)=2r^nE(r)-(n-2)u(r)y(r)
\]
and $E(r)>0$, we obtain $P(r)>-(n-2)u(r)y(r)$,
so $\liminf_{r\to\infty}P(r)\ge0$.  On the other hand, $h(u)<0$ for all
sufficiently small $u$.  Hence $P'<0$ eventually.  The function $P$ cannot
become nonpositive on that final interval.  Indeed, if $P(r_0)\le0$ at a
sufficiently large point, then strict decrease gives
$P(r)<P(r_1)< P(r_0)\leq 0$ for every $r>r_1>r_0$.  This contradicts the preceding
lower limit.  Thus $P(r)>0$ for all sufficiently large $r$.

Along the whole monotone tail, $h(u(r))$ changes sign at most once, from
positive to negative.                                                
Hence the same increase--decrease argument as in Lemma~\ref{lem:Ppositive} shows that \(P\) remains positive on the whole monotone tail. This proves the claim.

label: lem:inflection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:inflection}
Let $u$ be a monotone prezero half-phase, normalized so that $u>1$ and $u'<0$ between its initial critical point and the point where $u=1$. Assume $P_1>0$ on this interval. Then $u''$ vanishes exactly once there.  Before that point $u''<0$, and afterward $u''>0$.  In particular, $\lvertu'\rvert$ is strictly decreasing after the inflection point.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
At a positive-radius initial critical point, $u''=-f(u)<0$.  If the initial point is the origin, radial regularity gives $u''(0)=-f(\alpha)/n<0$.  At the level $u=1$, the equation gives $u''=-(n-1)u'/r>0$.  Hence a zero of $u''$ exists.  Let $r_0$ be the first one.  Then $u'''(r_0)\ge0$.  Differentiating the equation and using $u''(r_0)=0$ gives
\[
 u'''(r_0)=u'(r_0)
 \left(\frac{n-1}{r_0^2}-f'(u(r_0))\right),
\]
so, because $u'<0$,
\[
 \frac{n-1}{r_0^2}\le f'(u(r_0)).
\]
The inequality $u'''(r_0)\ge0$ is in fact strict. To see this, suppose
that $u'''(r_0)=0$ and put $u_0=u(r_0)>1$. Then
\[
 f'(u_0)=\frac{n-1}{r_0^2},\qquad
 f(u_0)=-\frac{n-1}{r_0}u'(r_0).
\]
Since $f$ is smooth near $u_0$, we may differentiate again. Since
\[
s\varpi'(s)
=1-\varpi(s)-\frac{f(s)f''(s)}{f'(s)^2},
\]
the strict positivity of $\varpi'(u_0)$ yields
\[
\frac{f(u_0)f''(u_0)}{f'(u_0)^2}
<1-\varpi(u_0)<1.
\]
Differentiating the equation twice and using
$u''(r_0)=u'''(r_0)=0$, we obtain
\[
u^{(4)}(r_0)
=-\frac{2(n-1)}{r_0^3}u'(r_0)
-f''(u_0)u'(r_0)^2=-\frac{u'(r_0)f'(u_0)}{r_0}
\left(
2-\frac{f(u_0)f''(u_0)}{f'(u_0)^2}
\right)>0.
\]
                                             
   
                                  
                   
   
              
   
              
                              
                                                    
   
Taylor's expansion yields
\[
u''(r)=\frac12u^{(4)}(r_0)(r-r_0)^2
+o((r-r_0)^2)>0
\]
for $r<r_0$ sufficiently close to $r_0$. This contradicts the negativity of $u''$ to the left of its first zero. Hence $u'''(r_0)>0$,
                                                                    
                                                             
               
and $u''$ crosses from negative to positive at $r_0$.

The equation at $r_0$ also yields
\[
 \omega(r_0)=-\frac{r_0u'(r_0)}{u(r_0)}
 =\frac{r_0^2 f(u(r_0))}{(n-1)u(r_0)}
 \geq \varpi(u(r_0)).
\]
Now $P_1>0$ implies that $\omega$ increases with $r$, while \eqref{eq:varpi} and the decrease of $u$ imply that $\varpi(u(r))$ decreases.  Thus
\[
 \omega(r)>\omega(r_0) \geq \varpi(u(r_0)) >\varpi(u(r)),\qquad r>r_0.
\]
At any later zero of $u''$, we would have
\[
 u'''=u'f'(u)\left(\frac{\varpi(u)}{\omega}-1\right)>0.
\]
If this were the first later zero, then $u''>0$ immediately to its left and hence $u'''\le0$ there.  This contradicts the displayed strict positivity.  Thus a second zero is impossible.  The final assertion follows from $u'<0$ and $u''>0$ after $r_0$.

label: eq:connection
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Expanding the left-hand side gives
\begin{align*}
 Q-P\frac vu
 &=r^n\left(u'v'-\frac{u'^2v}{u}
       +f(u)v-2F(u)\frac vu\right)\\
 &=r^n u'\left(v'-\frac{u'v}{u}\right)
   +r^n\frac vu\bigl(uf(u)-2F(u)\bigr)\\
 &=\left(-\frac{ru'}u\right)
   \left[r^{n-1}(u'v-uv')
    -r^{n-1}\frac{h_1(u)v}{u'}\right]\\
 &=\omega(M-\theta).
\end{align*}
This proves \eqref{eq:connection}.  Since
$h_1'=sf'(s)-f(s)$ and $g_2=2F/h_1$,
\[
 g_2'(s)h_1(s)=2f(s)-g_2(s)\bigl(sf'(s)-f(s)\bigr).
\]
Using \eqref{eq:Mprime}--\eqref{eq:Qprime} therefore yields
\eqref{eq:T2prime-regular}.  Substitution of the definition of $\theta$
gives \eqref{eq:T2prime} away from critical points.  Moreover,
\[
 B_0=Q-g_2(u)\theta,\qquad
 T_2-B_0=-g_2(u)(M-\theta).
\]
The equality
\[
 M-\theta=-\frac{T_2'}{g_2'(u)u'}
\]
then gives \eqref{eq:T2B0} wherever $u'\ne0$.

title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md: By the definition, $F_a(\pm A)=F_a(A)=F(A)-g_2(A)h_1(A)/2=0$.  Since $F_a$ is a linear combination of the two powers $\lverts\rvert^{p+1}$ and $\lverts\rvert^{q+1}$, the vanishing at $A$ forces the stated factorization.  If $A=\beta$, then $g_2(A)=0$; if $A>\beta$, then $0<g_2(A)<2/(p-1)<2/(q-1)$.  Hence $C_A>0$ in either case.

label: thm:firstphase
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:firstphase}

Let $u=u(\cdot,\alpha)$ be a bound state of \eqref{eq:shoot}.
Assume that $u$ has a first zero $z_1$ and a
first postzero critical point $c_1>z_1$.
Let $r_1\in(0,z_1)$ be the point at which $u(r_1)=1$.  Then the variation
$v=\partial_\alpha u$ has exactly one zero $\tau_1\in(0,r_1)$
on $[0,c_1]$.  More precisely,
\[
 v>0\quad\text{on }[0,\tau_1),
 \qquad
 v<0\quad\text{on }(\tau_1,c_1].
\]
In addition,
\begin{equation*}
 Q(c_1),\ M(c_1)>0,
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:first-Q12}
Q>0\quad\text{on }(0,r_1]\cup [\bar b_1,c_1],\qquad M,T_1>0\quad\text{on } (0,r_1],\qquad Q_1, Q_2>0
\quad \text{on } (0,c_1].
\end{equation}
Moreover
\begin{equation*}
  Q(\bar b_1)>Q(b_1)>0.
\end{equation*}
head: environment

label: eq:firstphase-energy-positive
title: Proof
body_md:
From Lemma~\ref{lem:nodal-geometry}, we obtain $\alpha>\beta$, $u(c_1)<-\beta$ and $u'<0$ on $(0,c_1)$.
This implies that
all four level points below are well defined and unique:
\begin{equation*}
 \begin{gathered}
 u(b_1)=\beta,\qquad u(r_1)=1,
 \qquad 0<b_1<r_1<z_1,\\
 u(\bar r_1)=-1,\qquad u(\bar b_1)=-\beta,
 \qquad z_1<\bar r_1<\bar b_1<c_1.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation*}
Moreover, by $u(c_1)<-\beta$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:firstphase-energy-positive}
 E(r)>E(c_1)=F(u(c_1))>0,\qquad 0\le r< c_1.
\end{equation}

We divide the argument into five steps.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 1: the first zero occurs before the level $u=1$.}
If $v$ had no zero on $(0,r_1)$, then $v>0$ on $[0,r_1)$ and, by continuity, $v(r_1)\ge0$.  Since $u>1$, \eqref{eq:high-signs} and \eqref{eq:rhoprime} give $\rho'>0$ on $(0,r_1)$, hence $\rho(r_1)>\rho(0)=0$.  But $f(1)=0$, $f'(1)=p-q>0$, and $u'(r_1)<0$, so
\[
 \rho(r_1)=r_1^{n-1}f'(1)u'(r_1)v(r_1)\le0,
\]
a contradiction.  Thus $v$ has a first zero $\tau_1\in(0,r_1)$, and $v'(\tau_1)<0$.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 2: there is no second zero while $u\geq1$.}
Before $\tau_1$, $f>0$, $uf'-f>0$, and $v>0$, so $Q',M'>0$.  Moreover
\[
 (r^{n-1}v')'=-r^{n-1}f'(u)v<0
\]
and $v'(0)=0$, hence $v'<0$.  Since $Q(0)=M(0)=T_1(0)=0$ and
\[
 T_1'=-g_1'(u)u'M,
\]
we obtain $Q,M,T_1>0$ on $(0,\tau_1]$.

Suppose that either $M$ ceases to be positive or $v$ has a second zero on
$(\tau_1,r_1]$, and let $s_*$ be the first such event.  At $\tau_1$, $M(\tau_1)>0$.
If $v$ had a second zero $\sigma\le r_1$ before $M$ vanished, then
$v'(\sigma)>0$ and
\[
 M(\sigma)=-\sigma^{n-1}u(\sigma)v'(\sigma)<0.
\]
Thus $M$ would already have vanished at an earlier point.  Hence the first
event must satisfy
\[
 M(s_*)=0,\qquad v(s_*)<0.
\]
On $(\tau_1,s_*)$, one has $M>0$, and therefore
$T_1'=-g_1'(u)u'M>0$.  It follows that
\[
 Q(s_*)=T_1(s_*)>0.
\]
The equality $M(s_*)=0$ gives $u'v=uv'$, and direct substitution yields
\[
 P_1(s_*)=Q(s_*)\frac{u(s_*)}{v(s_*)}.
\]
Here $u(s_*)\ge1$ and $v(s_*)<0$, while
$P_1(s_*)>0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:Ppositive}.
The right-hand side is negative.  This contradiction excludes both events.
Consequently
\[
 M>0,\qquad v<0\quad\text{on }(\tau_1,r_1].
\]
Using $T_1'=-g_1'(u)u'M>0$ again, we obtain $T_1>0$ on $(\tau_1,r_1]$. Thus $Q=T_1+g_1M>0$ on $(\tau_1,r_1]$.

At $r_1$, $g_1(1)=0$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qr1-positive}
 Q(r_1)=T_1(r_1)>0.
\end{equation}
Since $u'v>0$ there, also $Q_1(r_1)>0$.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 3: the bridge $B_0$ rules out a second zero on $(r_1,z_1]$.}
Suppose that either $Q_1$ reaches zero or $v$ has a second zero on
$(r_1,z_1]$, and let $s_*$ be the first such event.  Before $s_*$,
\[
 v<0,\qquad Q_1>0,\qquad u'v>0,
\]
and hence $Q_n>Q_1>0$.  Since $F(u)<0$ on $(r_1,z_1)$,
\eqref{eq:B0prime} gives $B_0'>0$.  Also, by \eqref{eq:Qr1-positive},
\[
 B_0(r_1)=Q(r_1)-2F(1)\frac{r_1^{n-1}v(r_1)}{u'(r_1)}>0.
\]

The first event cannot be a zero of $v$.  Indeed, at a second zero, one has
$v'(s_*)>0$, and therefore
\[
 Q_1(s_*)=Q(s_*)=s_*^n u'(s_*)v'(s_*)<0.
\]
Thus $Q_1$ would have vanished strictly before $s_*$.
Consequently, the first event would have to satisfy
\[
 Q_1(s_*)=0,\qquad v(s_*)<0.
\]
Using $Q_1(s_*)=0$ in the definition of $B_0$, we obtain
\[
 B_0(s_*)=-2s_*^{n-1}\frac{v(s_*)}{u'(s_*)}E(s_*)<0,
\]
where \eqref{eq:firstphase-energy-positive} gives $E(s_*)>0$.  This contradicts
$B_0(s_*)>B_0(r_1)>0$.  Hence neither event occurs on $(r_1,z_1]$.
Consequently, $v$ has exactly one zero on $(0,z_1)$ and $v(z_1)<0$.

The same argument also records the $Q$-family signs.  On $(0,\tau_1]$, $Q_1',Q_2'>0$.  On $(\tau_1,r_1]$, $Q>0$ and $u'v>0$, hence $Q_2>Q_1>Q>0$.  On $(r_1,z_1]$, the bridge argument gives $Q_1>0$, and $Q_2>Q_1$ because $u'v>0$.  Thus
\begin{equation*}
 Q_1,Q_2>0\quad\text{on }(0,z_1].
\end{equation*}
In particular,
at $z_1$, the bridge identity $B_0(z_1)=Q(z_1)$ and the monotonicity from $r_1$ give
\begin{equation*}
Q(z_1)=B_0(z_1)>B_0(r_1)>0.
\end{equation*}

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 4: passage through the postzero low-amplitude interval.}
On $(z_1,\bar b_1)$, one has $F<0$.  Suppose that either $Q_1$ reaches
zero or $v$ has a new zero on $(z_1,\bar b_1]$, and let $s_*$ be the first
event.  Before $s_*$, $v<0$, $Q_1>0$, and $u'v>0$,
so $Q_n>Q_1>0$.  Thus \eqref{eq:B0prime} gives $B_0'>0$ on $(z_1,\bar b_1)$.

If the first event were a zero of $v$, then $v'(s_*)>0$ and
\[
 Q_1(s_*)=Q(s_*)=s_*^n u'(s_*)v'(s_*)<0.
\]
Thus $Q_1$ would have reached zero earlier.  Hence the first event would have to satisfy $Q_1(s_*)=0$ with
$v(s_*)<0$.  As in Step~3,
\[
 B_0(s_*)=-2s_*^{n-1}\frac{v(s_*)}{u'(s_*)}E(s_*)<0,
\]
whereas $B_0(s_*)> B_0(z_1)=Q(z_1)>0$.  This contradiction proves
\[
 v<0,\qquad Q_2>Q_1>0\quad\text{on }(z_1,\bar b_1].
\]
In particular, since $F(-\beta)=0$,
\[
 Q(\bar b_1)=B_0(\bar b_1)>B_0(z_1)=Q(z_1)>0.
\]

We also record the comparison between the two points at the level $\lvertu\rvert=\beta$.  If $\tau_1\leq b_1$, then $u'v>0$ and $Q_n> Q_1>0$ on $(b_1,\bar b_1)$.  Since $F<0$ there, \eqref{eq:B0prime} gives $B_0'>0$.  Hence
\[
 Q(\bar b_1)=B_0(\bar b_1)>B_0(b_1)=Q(b_1)>0.
\]
Suppose next that $b_1<\tau_1$.  On $[b_1,\tau_1)$, one has $f(u)>0$ and $v>0$, so \eqref{eq:Qprime} gives $Q'>0$.  At $\tau_1$, one has $B_0(\tau_1)=Q(\tau_1)$. While on $(\tau_1,\bar b_1)$, one has $u'v>0$ and $Q_n>Q_1>0$.
This with $F<0$
 gives $B_0'>0$ on $(\tau_1,\bar b_1)$.
Therefore
\[
 Q(\bar b_1)=B_0(\bar b_1)>B_0(\tau_1)=Q(\tau_1)>Q(b_1)>0.
\]
Thus $Q(\bar b_1)>Q(b_1)>0$ in both cases.

On $(\bar b_1,c_1]$, we have $u<-\beta$, hence $f(u)<0$.  A further zero $\sigma$ of $v$ would force $Q'=2r^{n-1}f(u)v>0$ on $(\bar b_1,\sigma)$ and $Q(\sigma)=\sigma^n u'(\sigma)v'(\sigma)<0$, which is impossible since $Q(\bar b_1)>0$.  Hence $v<0$ all the way to $c_1$, $Q_2(c_1)=Q_1(c_1)=Q(c_1)>0$, and $Q_2>Q_1>Q>0$ on $(\bar b_1,c_1)$, proving \eqref{eq:first-Q12}.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 5: recovery of $M(c_1)>0$.}
At $\bar r_1$, $f(-1)=0$ and $f'(-1)=p-q>0$.  Since $u'v>0$,
\[
 \rho(\bar r_1)=\bar r_1^{n-1}f'(-1)u'(\bar r_1)v(\bar r_1)>0.
\]
On $(\bar r_1,c_1)$, one has $u<-1$, hence $f''(u)<0$, while $v<0$; thus \eqref{eq:rhoprime} gives $\rho'>0$.  At $c_1$,
\[
 0<\rho(c_1)=-c_1^{n-1}f(u(c_1))v'(c_1).
\]
Since $f(u(c_1))<0$, we have $v'(c_1)>0$, and therefore
\[
 M(c_1)=-c_1^{n-1}u(c_1)v'(c_1)>0.
\]
This completes the proof.

label: lem:prep
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
On $[c_-,\tau]$, $Q$ and $M$
increase by \eqref{eq:Mprime}--\eqref{eq:Qprime}, thus $Q,M>0$.
At $c_-$, the identity
\eqref{eq:T2prime-regular} gives
\[
 T_2'(c_-)=c_-^{n-1}g_2'(u(c_-))h_1(u(c_-))v(c_-)>0.
\]
For $c_-<s\le\tau$, one has $u'<0$, $\theta\le0<M$, and
$g_2'(u)>0$.
Hence $T_2'>0$ on $[c_-,\tau]$, then $T_2>0$.

If $\tau\ge b$, $Q_1,Q_2$ increase by the sign record. Then $Q_j\geq Q_j(c_-)=Q(c_-)>0$ on $[c_-,\tau]$, $j=1,2$.  Suppose $\tau<b$ and assume that $v$ has a second zero $\widetilde\tau\le b$.  At the first zero,
\[
 0<T_2(\tau)=\tau^{n-1}u(\tau)v'(\tau)
 \bigl[g_2(u(\tau))-\omega(\tau)\bigr].
\]
Since $u(\tau)v'(\tau)<0$, we have $g_2(u(\tau))<\omega(\tau)$.  On $(\tau,\widetilde\tau)$, the amplitude decreases, so $g_2(u)$ decreases. On $\lvertu\rvert>1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:Ppositive} gives $\omega'>0$.  At the second zero, $u(\widetilde\tau)v'(\widetilde\tau)>0$ and
 \begin{equation*}
 g_2(u(\widetilde\tau))-\omega(\widetilde\tau)<g_2(u(\tau))-\omega(\tau)<0,
\end{equation*}
hence the same formula would give $T_2(\widetilde\tau)<0$.
Since $T_2'(\tau)>0$, we know that,
before reaching $\widetilde\tau$, there is a first point $t_*$ at which $T_2'=0$ while $T_2>0$.  Formula \eqref{eq:T2prime} gives $M=\theta>0$ there.  Since $uv<0$ and $P>0$, the connection identity gives
\[
 Q=P\frac vu<0.
\]
But $T_2=Q-g_2M>0$ and $M>0$ imply $g_2<0$, equivalently $F<0$, whereas $t_*<b$ and hence $F>0$. Thus, $v$ has no zero on $(\tau,b]$. Moreover,
 this contradiction also shows that $T_2'$ cannot vanish before $b$.  Thus \eqref{eq:T2-prep} holds.

 On $(\tau,b]$, one has $u'v>0$ and $Q'=2r^{n-1}fv<0$, while $Q(b)=T_2(b)>0$ because $g_2(\beta)=0$.  Hence $Q>0$ on $(\tau,b]$, and therefore $Q_2>Q_1>Q>0$.

We also record that $M$ cannot vanish on $(\tau,b]$.  Indeed, at a first such zero $r_m$, the already established positivity of $T_2$ gives $Q(r_m)=T_2(r_m)>0$.  Since $M(r_m)=0$ means $u'v=uv'$, direct substitution in the definitions gives
\[
 P_1(r_m)=Q(r_m)\frac{u(r_m)}{v(r_m)}.
\]
Here $u>1$ and $v<0$, whereas $P_1>0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:Ppositive}; this is impossible.  Hence $M>0$ on $(\tau,b]$.

label: lem:Qn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Qn}
Assume \eqref{eq:ind-data}. Suppose that $Q_1>0$ on $[c_-,c_+]$.  If either
\[
 n\ge4,
 \qquad\text{or}\qquad
 n=3\ \text{ and }\ p+q\ge3,
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qnpositive}
 Q_n>0\quad\text{on }[b,c_+].
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The assumption $Q_1>0$ excludes a second zero of $v$.  Indeed, at such a
zero, one would have $v'>0$ and
\[
 Q_1=r^n u'v'<0.
\]
Consequently, $v<0$ after $\tau$, and hence $u'v>0$ on $(\tau,c_+)$.  Thus
$Q_n>Q_1>0$ there.  At $\tau$ and $c_+$, one has
$Q_n=Q_1>0$.  Suppose that \eqref{eq:Qnpositive} fails.  By continuity,
$Q_n$ has a zero in $[b,\tau)$.  Let $s_0$ be its largest zero there.  Then
\[
 b\le s_0<\tau,\qquad Q_n(s_0)=0,
 \qquad Q_n>0\quad\hbox{on }(s_0,c_+].
\]

At $c_-$,
$\rho(c_-)>0$.  On $(c_-,\tau)$,
$\rho'>0$, so
$\rho(s_0)>0$.  At $s_0$, the equality $Q_n(s_0)=0$ reads
\[
 -u'v=\frac{s_0}{2(n-1)}\bigl(u'v'+f(u)v\bigr).
\]
The right-hand side is positive.  Moreover, $\rho(s_0)>0$ gives
\[
 -f(u)v'>-f'(u)u'v
 =\frac{s_0f'(u)}{2(n-1)}\bigl(u'v'+f(u)v\bigr)
 >\frac{s_0f'(u)}{2(n-1)}u'v'.
\]
Here all functions are evaluated at $s_0$.  Dividing by $-v'(s_0)>0$ and
using $\omega=-ru'/u$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:add}
 \frac{2(n-1)f(u(s_0))}{u(s_0)f'(u(s_0))}>\omega(s_0).
\end{equation}
At $b$, $F(u(b))=0$ and $P(b)>0$, we obtain $\omega(b)>n-2$ from
  \begin{equation*}
    0<P(b)=b^nu'^2+(n-2)b^{n-1}uu'=b^{n-1}|u u'|\cdot[\omega(b)-(n-2)].
  \end{equation*}
  Since $b\leq s_0<r$, $1<u(s_0)\le\beta$ and $P_1>0$, so $\omega(s_0)\ge\omega(b)>n-2$.  With
\[
 x:=u(s_0)^{p-q}\in\left(1,\frac{p+1}{q+1}\right],
\]
from \eqref{eq:varpi} and \eqref{eq:add}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:xineq}
 \bigl[2(n-1)-(n-2)p\bigr]x
 >2(n-1)-(n-2)q.
\end{equation}

For $n\ge4$, the coefficient of $x$ is positive under $p<(n+2)/(n-2)$.  Using $x\le(p+1)/(q+1)$, \eqref{eq:xineq} would imply
\[
 \bigl[2(n-1)-(n-2)p\bigr](p+1)
 >\bigl[2(n-1)-(n-2)q\bigr](q+1).
\]
The difference of the left side and the right side equals
\begin{equation}\label{eq:param-Qn}
 -(p-q)\bigl((n-2)(p+q)-n\bigr).
\end{equation}
For $n\ge4$, one has $p+q>2\ge n/(n-2)$, so \eqref{eq:param-Qn} is nonpositive and we obtain a contradiction.  This calculation explains the auxiliary threshold $p+q\ge n/(n-2)$, but also shows why it imposes no extra condition once $n\ge4$.

Let $n=3$.  If $p\ge4$, then \eqref{eq:xineq} reads
\[
 (4-p)x>4-q.
\]
For $q<4$, the right-hand side is positive whereas the left is nonpositive.  For $q\ge4$, since $x>1$ and $p>q$, one has $(4-p)x<4-p<4-q$.  Both cases are impossible.  If $p<4$, the coefficient $4-p$ is positive and the same endpoint estimate as above gives a contradiction precisely when $p+q\ge3$.  This proves the lemma.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:Qn-first}
Let the notation be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:firstphase}.  If either
\[
 n\ge4,
 \qquad\text{or}\qquad

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:firstphase} gives $Q_1>0$ on $(0,c_1]$ and
shows that $v$ has exactly one zero $\tau_1$.  If $\tau_1\le b_1$, then
$u'v\ge0$ on $[b_1,c_1]$, with equality only at $\tau_1$ and $c_1$.
Hence $Q_n\ge Q_1>0$ there.

Suppose that $b_1<\tau_1$.
Then $Q_n\geq Q_1>0$ on $[\tau_1,c_1]$.
 If the conclusion failed, continuity
would give a largest zero
$s_0\in[b_1,\tau_1)$.  On $(0,\tau_1)$, one has $u>1$, $v>0$, and
\[
 \rho(0)=0,\qquad
 \rho'=r^{n-1}f''(u)u'^2v>0.
\]
Thus $\rho(s_0)>0$.  Since $s_0\geq b_1$, the equality $Q_n(s_0)=0$ and the
preceding calculation give
\[
 \frac{2(n-1)f(u(s_0))}{u(s_0)f'(u(s_0))}>\omega(s_0)
 \ge\omega(b_1)>n-2.
\]
Hence \eqref{eq:xineq} holds.  The parameter calculation in
\eqref{eq:param-Qn} gives the same contradiction for $n\ge4$, or for
$n=3$ with $p+q\ge3$.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The integral mean formula gives
\[
 \log \beta
 =\frac1{p-q}\int_q^p\frac{\,\mathrm d t}{t+1}
 <\frac1{q+1}<\frac12,
\]
so $\beta<\sqrt e$.  By \eqref{eq:residual-auto}, $q<3/2$.  Put $t=(q+1)^{-1}\in(2/5,1/2)$.  If $3\beta\le4$, the second inequality in \eqref{eq:beta-basic-bounds} is immediate.  If $3\beta>4$, monotonicity in $\beta$ and the preceding exponential bound give
\begin{align*}
 \beta^{q-1}(3\beta-4)
 <e^{\frac{q-1}{q+1}}\left(3e^{\frac{1}{q+1}}-4\right)
 =3e^{1-t}-4e^{1-2t}
 <3\sqrt e-4<1.
\end{align*}
Here $3e^{1-t}-4e^{1-2t}$ is strictly increasing on $(2/5,1/2)$, because its derivative is $e^{1-2t}(8-3e^t)>0$ there.

Finally, $3(\beta-1)<3(\sqrt e-1)<2$.  Hence
\[
 y\longmapsto y\bigl(3(\beta-1)-y\bigr)
\]
is strictly decreasing for $y\ge1$.  Under \eqref{eq:kappa-window}, necessarily $\beta>4/3$, and therefore
\[
 \kappa\bigl(3(\beta-1)-\kappa\bigr)
 <3\beta-4.
\]
Multiplying by $\beta^{q-1}$ and using \eqref{eq:beta-basic-bounds} proves \eqref{eq:kappa-weight-bound}.

label: lem:residual
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
On $(b,\tau)$,
\[
 1<u< \beta,\qquad v>0,\qquad u'<0,\qquad v'<0,\qquad M>0.
\]
We organize the proof in seven steps.  They are the double-power
counterparts of the residual comparison                 
\cite[Lemma~5.4]{Tang2026}.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 1: logarithmic slopes and the decreasing ratio $\mathcal R$.}
Since $P(b)>0$ and $F(\beta)=0$, we have $\omega(b)>n-2=1$.
Moreover $P_1>0$ on $u>1$, so $\omega$ is strictly increasing.  From $M>0$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:aomega}
 a(r):=-\frac{rv'(r)}{v(r)}>\omega(r)>\omega(b)>1.
\end{equation}
Set
\[
 \mathcal R(r):=\frac{f(u(r))v(r)}{u'(r)v'(r)}>0.
\]
For $x=u^d$,
\[
 \frac{3f(u)}{u f'(u)}=\frac{3(x-1)}{px-q}.
\]
The right-hand side increases with $x$, and $x< \beta^d=(p+1)/(q+1)$; hence
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{3f(u)}{u f'(u)}<\frac{3}{p+q+1}<1<\omega.
\end{equation*}
A direct differentiation using the equations for $u$ and $v$ gives
\begin{align*}
 u'v'\mathcal R'
 &=f'u'v+fv'
 +\mathcal R\left(\frac4r u'v'+fv'+f'u'v\right)\\
 &<f'u'v+fv'+\frac4r fv\\
 &=\frac{fv}{r}\left(\frac{rv'}v+1\right)
 +\frac{f'uv}{r}\left(\frac{3f}{uf'}-\omega\right)<0.
\end{align*}
Since $u'v'>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Rdecrease}
 \mathcal R'(r)<0 \quad \text{on }(b,\tau).
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 2: the sign pattern of $Q_3$.}
For $n=3$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Q3prime}
 Q_3'=r^2\bigl(3u'v'-fv\bigr)
 =r^2u'v'(3-\mathcal R).
\end{equation}
If $Q_3\ge0$ on $[b,\tau]$, by \eqref{eq:Qfamily-prep},
\[
 Q_3(\tau)=Q(\tau)>0.
\]
Moreover
$u(\tau)<\beta\le A$, so all other factors in the integrand of
\eqref{eq:residual-integral} are strictly positive in a left neighborhood
of $\tau$.  Hence the integral is strictly positive.  Suppose therefore
that $Q_3$ is negative somewhere on $(b,\tau)$.  Equation \eqref{eq:Rdecrease} shows that
$3-\mathcal R$ is strictly increasing.  Thus $Q_3'$ has at most one zero.
If it has one, its sign changes from negative to positive.  The zero is
therefore the absolute minimum point $r_0$ of $Q_3$.  At this point
$\mathcal R(r_0)=3$ (equivalently, $3u'(r_0)v'(r_0)=f(u(r_0))v(r_0)$), and
\begin{align*}
 \frac{Q_3(r_0)}{r_0^2}=&r_0\bigl(u'(r_0)v'(r_0)+f(u(r_0))v(r_0)\bigr)+4u'(r_0)v(r_0)
 \\=&4r_0u'(r_0)v'(r_0)+4u'(r_0)v(r_0)
 =4u'(r_0)v(r_0)
 \left(1+\frac{r_0v'(r_0)}{v(r_0)}\right)>0
\end{align*}
by \eqref{eq:aomega}.  This value is positive.  It contradicts the
assumed negative value of $Q_3$, because $r_0$ would be its absolute
minimum.  Hence $Q_3'$ has no zero.  Since
$Q_3'(\tau)=3\tau^2u'(\tau)v'(\tau)>0$, it follows that $Q_3'>0$
on $(b,\tau)$.  The negative set is an initial interval.  The
positivity of $Q_3(\tau)=Q(\tau)$ now gives a unique
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sigma}
 \sigma\in(b,\tau),\qquad
 Q_3<0 \quad \text{on }[b,\sigma),\qquad
 Q_3(\sigma)=0,\qquad
 Q_3>0 \quad \text{on }(\sigma,\tau].
\end{equation}
Since $u'v'>0$ and $Q_3'>0$ on $(b,\tau)$, identity
\eqref{eq:Q3prime} also gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:R-window}
 0<\mathcal R(r)<3\quad \text{on }(b,\tau).
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 3: the speed $\lvertu'\rvert$ decreases on the residual interval.}
Lemma~\ref{lem:inflection} gives a unique inflection point on the prezero
interval $u>1$.  Before this point $u''<0$, and after it $u''>0$.  If the
point were at or to the right of $b$, then $u''(b)\le0$.  The equation for
$u$ would give
\begin{equation*}
 -\frac{2u'(b)v(b)}{b}\le f(\beta)v(b).
\end{equation*}
Since $Q_3(b)<0$ by \eqref{eq:sigma},
\[
 b\bigl(u'v'+fv\bigr)<-4u'v\le2b fv,
\]
and hence $u'v'+fv>2u'v'>0$.  On the other hand,
$\rho(c_-)>0$, and on $(c_-,b)$,
$\rho'>0$, so
$\rho(b)>0$. Then
\[
 -fv'>-f'u'v
 >\frac{b f'}4\bigl(u'v'+fv\bigr)
 >\frac{b f'}2u'v'.
\]
Dividing by $-v'(b)>0$
yields
\[
 \frac{2f(\beta)}{\beta f'(\beta)}>\omega(b)>1.
\]
But $\beta^d=(p+1)/(q+1)$ gives the exact identity
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{2f(\beta)}{\beta f'(\beta)}=\frac{2}{p+q+1}<1,
\end{equation*}
a contradiction.  Thus the inflection point lies strictly before $b$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:speed-decrease}
 \lvertu'(r)\rvert\text{ is strictly decreasing on }(b,\tau).
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 4: quantitative separation of the positive and negative $Q_3$ regions.}
Since $v'<0$ and
\[
 (r^2v')'=-r^2f'(u)v<0,
\]
the function $r^2\lvertv'\rvert$ is strictly increasing.  Integrating \eqref{eq:Q3prime} from $\sigma$ to $\tau$ gives
\begin{align*}
\tau^3\lvertu'(\tau)v'(\tau)\rvert= Q_3(\tau)
 <3\int_\sigma^\tau r^2\lvertu'v'\rvert\,\mathrm d r<3\tau^2\lvertv'(\tau)\rvert\bigl(u(\sigma)-u(\tau)\bigr).
\end{align*}
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S6general}
 3\bigl(u(\sigma)-u(\tau)\bigr)>\tau\lvertu'(\tau)\rvert.
\end{equation}
Put
\[
 S:=u(\sigma)> T:=u(\tau)>1,\qquad \omega(\tau)>\omega(b)>1,
 \qquad \kappa:=\frac{\omega(\tau)}{\omega(b)}>1.
\]
Then \eqref{eq:S6general} gives
\begin{equation*}
S-T>\frac{\tau\lvertu'(\tau)\rvert}{3}>\frac{\tau\lvertu'(\tau)\rvert}{3u(\tau)\omega(b)}=-\frac{\tau{u'(\tau)}}{3u(\tau)\omega(b)}=\frac{\kappa}{3}.
\end{equation*}
 In particular, $\kappa<3(\beta-1)$ because
$S-T<\beta-T<\beta-1$.  Also
\[
 (\beta-S)+(S-T)=\beta-T<\beta-1.
\]
Thus $\beta-S<\beta-1-\kappa/3$, and hence
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{S-T}{\beta-S}
 >\frac{\kappa}{3(\beta-1)-\kappa},
 \qquad 1<\kappa<3(\beta-1).
\end{equation*}
The denominator is positive.  Lemma~\ref{lem:residual-parameter} gives
$\kappa\beta^{q-1}[3(\beta-1)-\kappa]<1$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-length}
 \frac{S-T}{\beta-S}
                                         
 >\kappa^2\beta^{q-1}.
\end{equation}
This is the point at which the double-power proof differs
quantitatively from the pure-power residual estimate in
\cite[Lemma~5.4]{Tang2026}: the factor $\beta^{q-1}$ is exactly what is
needed to absorb the additional weight below.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 5: equal-amplitude pairing of $Q_3$.}
The bound \eqref{eq:R-window} gives $0<\mathcal R(\sigma)<3$.
For $r^-\in[b,\sigma)$, define $r^+\in(\sigma,\tau)$ by
\[
 u(r^-)-S=S-u(r^+).
\]
This point exists and is unique.  Indeed,
\eqref{eq:weighted-length} implies $S-T>\beta-S$. Since $\mathcal{R}$ decreases and $r^2|v'|$ increases,
by $\,\mathrm d u=u'\,\mathrm d r$, integration of \eqref{eq:Q3prime} gives
\begin{align*}
 \lvertQ_3(r^-)\rvert=\int^\sigma_{r^-} r^2u'v'(3-\mathcal R)\,\mathrm d r<\bigl(3-\mathcal R(\sigma)\bigr)\int^\sigma_{r^-} r^2u'v'\,\mathrm d r
 &<\bigl(3-\mathcal R(\sigma)\bigr)\sigma^2\lvertv'(\sigma)\rvert
 \lvertu(r^-)-S\rvert,\\
 Q_3(r^+)=\int_\sigma^{r^+} r^2u'v'(3-\mathcal R)\,\mathrm d r>\bigl(3-\mathcal R(\sigma)\bigr)\int_\sigma^{r^+} r^2u'v'\,\mathrm d r
 &>\bigl(3-\mathcal R(\sigma)\bigr)\sigma^2\lvertv'(\sigma)\rvert
 \lvertS-u(r^+)\rvert,
\end{align*}
and hence
\begin{equation*}
 Q_3(r^+)>\lvertQ_3(r^-)\rvert.
\end{equation*}

Define normalized points $\widetilde r_x\in[b,\sigma]$ and $\widehat r_x\in[\sigma,\tau]$ by
\[
 u(\widetilde r_x)=S+(\beta-S)x,
 \qquad
 u(\widehat r_x)=S-(S-T)x,
 \qquad 0\le x\le1.
\]
For $x>0$, the amplitude drop from $S$ to $u(\widehat r_x)$ is
$(S-T)x$.  The drop paired with $\widetilde r_x$ is $(\beta-S)x$.  Since
$S-T>\beta-S$, $\widehat r_x$ lies strictly to the right of that
equal-amplitude partner.  The strict increase of $Q_3$ and the preceding
paired estimate give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normalized-pair}
 Q_3(\widehat r_x)>\lvertQ_3(\widetilde r_x)\rvert,\qquad
 0<x\le1.
\end{equation}
                  
            
             
\textbf{Step 6: the weighted $Q_3$ mass and its quantitative margin.}
Use the normalized points from Step~5 and set
\[
 U_-(x)=S+(\beta-S)x,\qquad U_+(x)=S-(S-T)x.
\]
The changes of variable $\,\mathrm d r=\,\mathrm d u/u'$ give
\begin{align*}
 \int_b^\sigma u^{q-1}\lvertQ_3\rvert\,\mathrm d r
 &=(\beta-S)\int_0^1
 \frac{U_-(x)^{q-1}\lvertQ_3(\widetilde r_x)\rvert}
 {\lvertu'(\widetilde r_x)\rvert}\,\mathrm d x,\\
 \int_\sigma^\tau u^{q-1}Q_3\,\mathrm d r
 &=(S-T)\int_0^1
 \frac{U_+(x)^{q-1}Q_3(\widehat r_x)}
 {\lvertu'(\widehat r_x)\rvert}\,\mathrm d x.
\end{align*}
For $0<x\le1$, the speed decrease in \eqref{eq:speed-decrease} gives
\[
 \lvertu'(\widetilde r_x)\rvert>
 \lvertu'(\sigma)\rvert>
 \lvertu'(\widehat r_x)\rvert.
\]
Also $U_-(x)\le\beta$ and $U_+(x)\ge T>1$, so
\[
 U_+(x)^{q-1}>\beta^{-(q-1)}U_-(x)^{q-1}.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:normalized-pair}, these inequalities yield
\begin{align*}
 \int_\sigma^\tau u^{q-1}Q_3\,\mathrm d r
 >\frac{S-T}{\beta^{q-1}\lvertu'(\sigma)\rvert}
   \int_0^1 U_-(x)^{q-1}\lvertQ_3(\widetilde r_x)\rvert\,\mathrm d x
 >\frac{S-T}{\beta^{q-1}(\beta-S)}
   \int_b^\sigma u^{q-1}\lvertQ_3\rvert\,\mathrm d r.
\end{align*}
The integrands are strictly positive for $x>0$, so both integrated
inequalities are strict. By \eqref{eq:weighted-length},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-Q3-mass}
 \int_\sigma^\tau u^{q-1}Q_3\,\mathrm d r
                              
                                       
 >\kappa^2\int_b^\sigma u^{q-1}\lvertQ_3\rvert\,\mathrm d r.
\end{equation}
                                                              
                                                                     
              

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Step 7: insertion of the bridge weight.}
Put
\[
 K_A(u):=1-\left(\frac{u}{A}\right)^d.
\]
Since $A\ge \beta>S$, $K_A(S)>0$, and $K_A(u(r))$ increases with $r$ on
$(b,\tau)$.  Using $u'^2=\omega^2u^2/r^2$, the integral in
\eqref{eq:residual-integral} is
\[
 \int_b^\tau u^{q-1}K_A(u)\frac{rQ_3}{\omega^2}\,\mathrm d r.
\]
On $[b,\sigma]$, one has $Q_3\le0$ and
\[
 \frac{rK_A(u)}{\omega^2}
 \le\frac{\sigma K_A(S)}{\omega(b)^2}
 =\frac{\sigma K_A(S)\kappa^2}{\omega(\tau)^2}.
\]
On $[\sigma,\tau]$, one has $Q_3\ge0$ and
\[
 \frac{rK_A(u)}{\omega^2}
 \ge\frac{\sigma K_A(S)}{\omega(\tau)^2}.
\]
The inequalities are strict away from $\sigma$.  Splitting the integral at
$\sigma$ and respecting the opposite signs of $Q_3$ therefore gives
\begin{align*}
 \int_b^\tau u^{q-1}K_A(u)\frac{rQ_3}{\omega^2}\,\mathrm d r>\frac{\sigma K_A(S)}{\omega(\tau)^2}
 \left[
 \int_\sigma^\tau u^{q-1}Q_3\,\mathrm d r
 -\kappa^2\int_b^\sigma u^{q-1}\lvertQ_3\rvert\,\mathrm d r
 \right]>0
\end{align*}
by \eqref{eq:weighted-Q3-mass}.  This proves \eqref{eq:residual-integral}.

Theorem~\ref{thm:firstphase}. \emph{If $b_1<\tau_1$}, then for every

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\tau_1\le b_1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:firstphase} gives
$v\le0$ on $[b_1,c_1]$ and $u'<0$ on $[b_1,c_1)$; hence
$Q_3=Q_1+2r^2u'v\ge Q_1>0$.
Now assume $b_1<\tau_1$.  Theorem~\ref{thm:firstphase} gives
$Q,M>0$ on $[b_1,\tau_1]$, while
\[
 \rho(0)=0,\qquad
 \rho'=r^{n-1}f''(u)u'^2v>0
 \quad\text{on }(0,b_1].
\]
Thus $\rho(b_1)>0$.  These are the initial signs used in
Lemma~\ref{lem:residual}; its proof applies on the interval $[b_1,\tau_1]$ without any other changes.

label: add4.71
title: Proof
body_md:
Put $s_0:=\max\{\tau,b\}\geq b$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:prep} gives $Q,Q_1,Q_2>0$ on $[c_-,s_0]$ and
excludes a second zero of $v$ before $s_0$.
The simultaneous continuation argument in Steps~3--4 of
Theorem~\ref{thm:firstphase} applies on $(s_0,\bar b]$.
Indeed, its initial and interval hypotheses are
\[
 B_0(s_0)=Q(s_0)>0,\qquad
 F(u)<0,\qquad E(r)>E(c_+)>0.
\]
As long as $v<0$ and $Q_1>0$, we have $Q_n>Q_1>0$ and
$B_0'>0$. At a second zero of $v$, $Q_1=r^nu'v'<0$;
at a first zero of $Q_1$ with $v<0$,
$B_0=-2r^{n-1}(v/u')E<0$. Both alternatives contradict the
preceding signs. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{add4.71}
  v<0,\qquad Q_2>Q_1>0
 \quad\text{on }(s_0,\bar b].
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{add4.72}
  Q(\bar b)=B_0(\bar b)>B_0(s_0)>0.
\end{equation}

On $(\bar b,c_+]$, a further zero $\sigma$ of $v$ would force $Q'>0$ on $(\bar b,\sigma)$ and $Q(\sigma)<0<Q(\bar b)$, which is impossible.  Hence $v<0$ on $(\bar b,c_+]$, $Q_2(c_+)=Q_1(c_+)=Q(c_+)>0$, and $Q_2>Q_1>Q>0$ on $(\bar b,c_+)$.
This together with \eqref{eq:Qfamily-prep}, \eqref{add4.71} and \eqref{add4.72}, proves
\eqref{eq:Q12all} and the last assertion in \eqref{eq:Qbb}.

It remains to compare $Q(b)$ and $Q(\bar b)$.  If $\tau\le b$, then
$Q_n>Q_1>0$ on $(b,\bar b)$, so \eqref{eq:B0prime} and $F<0$ give $Q(\bar b)=B_0(\bar b)>B_0(b)=Q(b)>0$.
If $b<\tau$, then $f(u)>0$ and $v>0$ on $[b,\tau)$, hence $Q(\tau)>Q(b)>0$.
On $(\tau,\bar b)$, $Q_n>Q_1>0$, and the same bridge argument yields $Q(\bar b)=B_0(\bar b)>B_0(\tau)=Q(\tau)$.
Thus in both cases $Q(\bar b)>Q(b)>0$.

label: lem:phi
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:phi}
Assume \eqref{eq:ind-data}.
For $\mu\in[\beta,A_+)$, let $r^-_\mu\in(c_-,b]$ and
$r^+_\mu\in[\bar b,c_+)$ be defined by
\[
 u(r^-_\mu)=\mu,
 \qquad
 u(r^+_\mu)=-\mu.
\]
Set
\[
 \Phi(r):=\frac{Q(r)}{r^{n-1}\lvertu'(r)\rvert}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi-comp}
 \Phi(r^+_\mu)>\Phi(r^-_\mu)>0
 \quad\text{for all }\mu\in[\beta,A_+).
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
\[
 \widehat E(r):=r^{2(n-1)}E(r).
\]
Using \eqref{eq:Eprime},
\begin{equation*}
 \widehat E'(r)=2(n-1)r^{2n-3}F(u(r)).
\end{equation*}
Since $F<0$ between $b$ and $\bar b$, and $F(\pm\beta)=0$,
\begin{equation*}
 (r^+_\beta)^{n-1}\lvertu'(r^+_\beta)\rvert
 <(r^-_\beta)^{n-1}\lvertu'(r^-_\beta)\rvert.
\end{equation*}
Together with $Q(\bar b)>Q(b)>0$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:river}, this proves \eqref{eq:Phi-comp} at $\mu=\beta$.

For $\mu\in[\beta,A_+)$, define
\[
 D(\mu):=\Phi(r^+_\mu)-\Phi(r^-_\mu)
\]
and set
\[
 \Phi_2(r):=\frac{Q_2(r)}{r^{n-1}\lvertu'(r)\rvert^3},
 \qquad
 D_2(\mu):=\Phi_2(r^+_\mu)-\Phi_2(r^-_\mu).
\]
We have already proved that $D(\beta)>0$.  We first show that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi2-comp}
 D(\mu)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D_2(\mu)>0.
\end{equation}
At equal amplitudes, strict energy decrease gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:speed-pair}
 \lvertu'(r^+_\mu)\rvert<\lvertu'(r^-_\mu)\rvert.
\end{equation}
If $r^-_\mu\le\tau$, then $u'v\le0$ at $r^-_\mu$, while $u'v>0$ at
$r^+_\mu$.  Hence
\[
 Q_2(r^-_\mu)\le Q(r^-_\mu),
 \qquad
 Q_2(r^+_\mu)>Q(r^+_\mu),
\]
and
$D(\mu)>0$,
\eqref{eq:speed-pair} give the explicit chain
\begin{align*}
 \Phi_2(r^+_\mu)
 &>\frac{Q(r^+_\mu)}{(r^+_\mu)^{n-1}
 \lvertu'(r^+_\mu)\rvert^3}
 =\frac{\Phi(r^+_\mu)}{\lvertu'(r^+_\mu)\rvert^2}\\
 &>\frac{\Phi(r^-_\mu)}{\lvertu'(r^-_\mu)\rvert^2}
 =\frac{Q(r^-_\mu)}{(r^-_\mu)^{n-1}
 \lvertu'(r^-_\mu)\rvert^3}
 \ge\Phi_2(r^-_\mu).
\end{align*}
Thus $D_2(\mu)>0$ in this case.

Assume next that $r^-_\mu>\tau$.  Then $u'v>0$ at $r^-_\mu$ and $r^+_\mu$.
Since $Q_1>0$ on $[c_-,c_+]$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:river}, integration of \eqref{eq:vuratio} from
$r^-_\mu$ to $r^+_\mu$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:vu-pair}
 \frac{v(r^+_\mu)}{u'(r^+_\mu)}
 >\frac{v(r^-_\mu)}{u'(r^-_\mu)}>0.
\end{equation}
At every point where $u'v>0$, one has
\[
 \Phi_2
 =\frac{\Phi}{\lvertu'\rvert^2}
 +\frac{2}{\lvertu'\rvert}\frac{v}{u'}.
\]
The first summand at $r^+_\mu$ is larger than the first summand at
$r^-_\mu$, because $D(\mu)>0$ and
\eqref{eq:speed-pair} hold.  The second summand is also larger, by
 \eqref{eq:speed-pair} and \eqref{eq:vu-pair}.  Hence
$D_2(\mu)>0$.  This proves
\eqref{eq:Phi2-comp}.

Suppose now that \eqref{eq:Phi-comp} fails.  By continuity, there is a first
contact $\mu_*\in(\beta,A_+)$ such that
\[
 D(\mu)>0\quad \text{on }(\beta,\mu_*),
 \qquad D(\mu_*)=0.
\]
On the prezero branch, parametrized by $s=u>0$, identity
\eqref{eq:Qratio} gives
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d s}\Phi(r^-_s)=f(s)\Phi_2(r^-_s).
\]
On the postzero branch, parametrized by $s=\lvertu\rvert=-u>0$, the oddness of $f$ gives the same formula
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d s}\Phi(r^+_s)=f(s)\Phi_2(r^+_s).
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi-integral}
 D(\mu_*)=D(\beta)+\int_\beta^{\mu_*}f(s)D_2(s)\,\mathrm d s.
\end{equation}
For $\beta<s<\mu_*$, one has $f(s)>0$, $D(s)>0$, and hence
$D_2(s)>0$ by \eqref{eq:Phi2-comp}.  The right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:Phi-integral} is therefore strictly positive.  This contradicts
$D(\mu_*)=0$, thus $\Phi(r^+_\mu)>\Phi(r^-_\mu)$ for all $\mu\in[\beta,A_+)$.
Finally, it follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:river} that $\Phi(r^-_\mu)>0$, and
proves \eqref{eq:Phi-comp}.

label: lem:renewal
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
On the postzero high-amplitude interval $[\bar b,c_+)$,
$u'v>0$, so $Q_n>Q_1>0$.
At $c_+$, one has $Q_n=Q_1=Q>0$.
At $\bar b$, $g_2(-\beta)=0$, hence $T_2(\bar b)=Q(\bar b)>0$.  Since
\[
 u(c_+)<-\beta,\qquad v(c_+)<0,\qquad g_2'(u(c_+))<0,\qquad h_1(u(c_+))>0,
\]
by \eqref{eq:T2prime-regular},
\[
 T_2'(c_+)
 =c_+^{n-1}g_2'(u(c_+))h_1(u(c_+))v(c_+)>0.
\]
Thus $T_2'>0$ on a left neighborhood of $c_+$.

If $t\in(\bar b,c_+)$ satisfies $T_2'(t)=0$, then $u'(t)\ne0$.
Differentiating \eqref{eq:T2B0}, using \eqref{eq:B0prime} and
$T_2'(t)=0$, first gives
\[
 0=B_0'(t)+\frac{g_2(u(t))}{g_2'(u(t))u'(t)}T_2''(t).
\]
Since $2F=g_2h_1$, this becomes
\begin{equation*}
 T_2''(t)=h_1(u(t))g_2'(u(t))u'(t)
 \frac{Q_n(t)}{t u'(t)^2}>0.
\end{equation*}
Indeed, $h_1(u(t))>0$ and $Q_n(t)>0$, while both $g_2'(u(t))$ and
$u'(t)$ are negative on this branch.  Hence every zero of $T_2'$ is
simple, and $T_2'$ crosses there from negative to positive.  There can be
at most one such zero.  Otherwise, after the first zero $t_1$, the derivative
$T_2'$ is positive.  If $t_2>t_1$ were the next zero, then $T_2'>0$
immediately to the left of $t_2$, whereas $T_2''(t_2)>0$ would force
$T_2'<0$ immediately to its left.  This is a contradiction.  If $T_2'$
has no zero in $(\bar b,c_+)$, its sign is constant there.  Its positivity
near $c_+$ implies $T_2'>0$ throughout this interval.  Hence
$T_2(c_+)>T_2(\bar b)>0$.

Suppose therefore that the unique critical point exists and denote it by
$t^+$.  It lies strictly between $\bar b$ and $c_+$.  The crossing
orientation gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T2postsign}
 T_2'<0\quad\text{on }(\bar b,t^+),
 \qquad T_2'(t^+)=0,\qquad
 T_2'>0\quad\text{on }(t^+,c_+).
\end{equation}
Put
\[
 A:=\lvertu(t^+)\rvert\in(\beta,A_+),
\]
and let $t^-\in(c_-,b)$ be the unique point with $u(t^-)=A$.  This point
exists because $A<A_+<A_-$ and $u$ is strictly decreasing.  Lemma~\ref{lem:prep}
gives $T_2(t^-)>0$.

Set $a=g_2(A)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{add4.92}
 H_A(s):=-2F_a(s)
 =C_A\lverts\rvert^{q+1}\left[1-\left(\frac{\lverts\rvert}{A}\right)^d\right]
 \begin{cases}
 =0,\qquad&\lverts\rvert=0, A,\\
 >0,\qquad&0<\lverts\rvert<A,
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
where $C_A>0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:factor}.
                                      
              
Since $F_a(\pm A)=0$, integration of \eqref{eq:Baprime} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T2integral}
 T_2(t^+)-T_2(t^-)
 =\int_{t^-}^{t^+}H_A(u(r))\frac{Q_n(r)}{r u'(r)^2}\,\mathrm d r.
\end{equation}
We show that the integral is strictly positive.

First pair the high-amplitude pieces $[t^-,b]$ and $[\bar b,t^+]$.  For $\mu\in[\beta,A]$, let $r^-_\mu$ and $r^+_\mu$ be the equal-amplitude points from Lemma~\ref{lem:phi} and set
\[
 \Psi(\mu):=
 \frac{Q_n(r^+_\mu)}{r^+_\mu\lvertu'(r^+_\mu)\rvert^3}
 +\frac{Q_n(r^-_\mu)}{r^-_\mu\lvertu'(r^-_\mu)\rvert^3}.
\]
We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Psi-positive}
 \Psi(\mu)>0\quad\text{for all }\mu\in(\beta,A).
\end{equation}
If $Q_n(r^-_\mu)\ge0$, this is immediate because $Q_n(r^+_\mu)>0$.  Assume $Q_n(r^-_\mu)<0$.  Then $r^-_\mu<\tau$.  On the prezero side, one has $\theta<0<M$, so the connection identity \eqref{eq:connection} and $uv>0$, $\omega>0$, $P,Q>0$ imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:connection-pre-pair}
{v(r^-_\mu)}
 <\frac{Q(r^-_\mu)}{P(r^-_\mu)}\,\mu.
\end{equation}
On the postzero interval $(\bar b,t^+)$, \eqref{eq:T2postsign} gives $T_2'<0$.
Since $g_2'(u)u'>0$, formula \eqref{eq:T2prime} gives $M>\theta$.  There $\omega<0$; hence \eqref{eq:connection} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:connection-pre-pair'}
 \lvertv(r^+_\mu)\rvert
 >\frac{Q(r^+_\mu)}{P(r^+_\mu)}\,\mu,
 \qquad \beta<\mu< A.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $Q_2(r^-_\mu)>0$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{add4.91}
 -Q_n(r^-_\mu)
 <(n-2)(r^-_\mu)^{n-1}\lvertu'(r^-_\mu)v(r^-_\mu)\rvert,
\end{equation}
whereas $u'v>0$ and $Q>0$ on the postzero side give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qn-post-bound}
 Q_n(r^+_\mu)
 >n(r^+_\mu)^{n-1}{u'(r^+_\mu)v(r^+_\mu)}.
\end{equation}

It remains to compare the coefficients in these two estimates.  Define
\[
 \mathcal S(r):=\frac{r^{n-2}Q(r)}{P(r)u'(r)^2}
 =\Phi(r)\,
 \frac{r^{n-3}}{\lvertu'(r)\rvert}\,
 \frac{r^n}{P(r)}.
\]
At equal amplitudes, Lemma~\ref{lem:phi} gives $\Phi(r^+_\mu)>\Phi(r^-_\mu)>0$; the energy decrease gives $\lvertu'(r^+_\mu)\rvert<\lvertu'(r^-_\mu)\rvert$; $P>0$ and $P/r^n$ is decreasing by Lemma~\ref{lem:Ppositive}.  Since $r^+_\mu>r^-_\mu$ and $n\ge3$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S-pair}
 \mathcal S(r^+_\mu)>\mathcal S(r^-_\mu)>0.
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{eq:connection-pre-pair}--\eqref{eq:Qn-post-bound} with \eqref{eq:S-pair} yields
\begin{align*}
 \frac{Q_n(r^+_\mu)}{r^+_\mu\lvertu'(r^+_\mu)\rvert^3}
 >n\mu\,\mathcal S(r^+_\mu)
 >(n-2)\mu\,\mathcal S(r^-_\mu)
 >\frac{-Q_n(r^-_\mu)}{r^-_\mu\lvertu'(r^-_\mu)\rvert^3},
\end{align*}
which proves \eqref{eq:Psi-positive}.

On $[t^-,b]$, the variable $\mu=u$ decreases from $A$ to $\beta$ and
$\,\mathrm d r=-\,\mathrm d\mu/\lvertu'\rvert$.  On $[\bar b,t^+]$, the variable
$\mu=-u$ increases from $\beta$ to $A$ and
$\,\mathrm d r=\,\mathrm d\mu/\lvertu'\rvert$.
By \eqref{add4.92} and \eqref{eq:Psi-positive}, using the evenness of $H_A$, we obtain
\begin{align}\label{eq:high-pair-positive}
 &\int_{t^-}^{b}H_A(u)\frac{Q_n}{r u'^2}\,\mathrm d r
 +\int_{\bar b}^{t^+}H_A(u)\frac{Q_n}{r u'^2}\,\mathrm d r
 \nonumber\\
 =&\int_A^\beta
 H_A(\mu)\frac{Q_n(r^-_\mu)}{r^-_\mu\lvertu'(r^-_\mu)\rvert^2}
 \left(-\frac{\,\mathrm d\mu}{\lvertu'(r^-_\mu)\rvert}\right)+\int^A_\beta
 H_A(\mu)\frac{Q_n(r^+_\mu)}{r^+_\mu\lvertu'(r^+_\mu)\rvert^2}
 \left(\frac{\,\mathrm d\mu}{\lvertu'(r^+_\mu)\rvert}\right)\nonumber
 \\
 =&\int_\beta^A H_A(\mu)
 \frac{Q_n(r^-_\mu)}{r^-_\mu\lvertu'(r^-_\mu)\rvert^3}\,\mathrm d\mu+\int_\beta^A H_A(\mu)
 \frac{Q_n(r^+_\mu)}{r^+_\mu\lvertu'(r^+_\mu)\rvert^3}\,\mathrm d\mu\nonumber\\=&
 \int_\beta^A H_A(\mu)\Psi(\mu)\,\mathrm d\mu>0.
\end{align}

            
             
                                                                       
                                                     
                                                                       
                                                                    
                                  
              
It remains to treat the middle interval $[b,\bar b]$.  If either $n\ge4$, or $n=3$ and $p+q\ge3$, Lemma~\ref{lem:Qn} gives $Q_n>0$ there, and hence the middle contribution is positive.  Suppose instead that $n=3$ and $p+q<3$.  If $\tau\le b$, then $Q_3\ge Q_1>0$ on $[b,\bar b]$.  If $b<\tau$, $Q_3>Q_1>0$ on $(\tau,\bar b]$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:residual} gives
\[
 \int_b^\tau H_A(u)\frac{Q_3}{r u'^2}\,\mathrm d r>0.
\]
Thus in every case
\begin{equation}\label{eq:middle-positive}
 \int_b^{\bar b}H_A(u)\frac{Q_n}{r u'^2}\,\mathrm d r>0.
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{eq:high-pair-positive} and \eqref{eq:middle-positive} in \eqref{eq:T2integral} gives
\[
 T_2(t^+)>T_2(t^-)>0.
\]
Thus the unique possible minimum of $T_2$ is positive, and $T_2(c_+)>0$.

\label{prop:phase}
Assume \eqref{eq:ind-data}. Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemmas~\ref{lem:prep} and~\ref{lem:river} give the unique zero of $v$ and the positivity of $Q_1,Q_2$ on $[c_-,c_+]$.  Lemmas~\ref{lem:river} and~\ref{lem:renewal} yield $Q(c_+)>0$ and $T_2(c_+)>0$.

It remains to recover $M(c_+)>0$.
At $\bar r$, $f=0$, $f'=p-q>0$, and $u'v>0$, hence $\rho(\bar r)>0$.  On $(\bar r,c_+)$, the signs of $f''(u)$ and $v$ agree, so \eqref{eq:rhoprime} gives $\rho'>0$.  Thus at $c_+$,
\[
 0<\rho(c_+)=-c_+^{n-1}f(u(c_+))v'(c_+),
\]
which forces $-u(c_+)v'(c_+)>0$ and therefore $M(c_+)>0$.

label: prop:terminal-tail
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:terminal-tail}
Set
\[
 Z(r):=-r^{n-1}u'(r).
\]
Then $Z>0$ on $[r_{*},\infty)$ and $Z$ is strictly
decreasing on $(r_{*},\infty)$.  Moreover, for every $r\ge r_{*}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:terminal-tail-basic}
 0<-u'(r)\le Z(r_{*})r^{1-n},
 \qquad
 0<u(r)\le \frac{Z(r_{*})}{n-2}r^{2-n}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $r\lvertu'(r)\rvert\rightarrow0$ as $r\to\infty$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:terminal-normalization}, $Z>0$.  Since $0<u<1$ on
$(r_{*},\infty)$,
\[
 Z'(r)=r^{n-1}f(u(r))
 =-r^{n-1}u(r)^q\bigl(1-u(r)^{p-q}\bigr)<0.
\]
Hence $0<Z(r)\le Z(r_{*})$, which gives the first estimate in
\eqref{eq:terminal-tail-basic}.  Using $u(r)\to0$ and $u'<0$,
\[
 u(r)=\int_r^\infty -u'(s)\,\,\mathrm d s
 \le Z(r_{*})\int_r^\infty s^{1-n}\,\,\mathrm d s
 =\frac{Z(r_{*})}{n-2}r^{2-n}.
\]
The last assertion follows from
$0<-ru'(r)\le Z(r_{*})r^{2-n}\to0$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:Ptail} gives $P>0$ on the whole terminal branch, while
$u\ge1$ on $[c_*,r_{*}]$ gives $P_1>0$ there.
From \eqref{eq:tail-ind-data},
\[
 v(c_*)>0,\qquad v'(c_*)<0.
\]
If $v$ stayed positive up to $r_{*}$, then the same $\rho$-argument as in
Section~\ref{sec:transition} would give
$\rho(r_{*})>0$, whereas
\[
 \rho(r_{*})
 =r_{*}^{n-1}f'(1)u'(r_{*})v(r_{*})\le0.
\]
Thus the first zero $\tau_{*}$ lies in $(c_*,r_{*})$; moreover the
variational equation gives $v'<0$ on $(c_*,\tau_{*})$.

From this point, the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:prep} is entirely local: it
uses only the interval from the initial critical point to the level
$u=\beta$, the positivity of $P$ and $P_1$, and the identities for
$Q,M,T_2,Q_1,Q_2$.  Applying that argument with
\[
 c_-=c_*,\qquad b=b_{*},\qquad r=r_{*}
\]
gives exactly \eqref{eq:tail-prep-conclusion} and excludes a second zero
of $v$ before $s_{**}$.

Furthermore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:terminal-transversality}

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{cor:variation-finite} gives the terminal induction data
\eqref{eq:tail-ind-data}.  Lemma~\ref{lem:tail-prep} therefore yields the
first zero $\tau_{*}$ on $[c_*,s_{**}]$ and, with
$s_{**}=\max\{\tau_{*},b_{*}\}$, gives
\[
 v<0, \ Q_1>0
 \quad\text{immediately to the right of }s_{**},
 \qquad
 B_0(s_{**})=Q(s_{**})>0.
\]
Here the last identity follows because either $v(s_{**})=0$ or
$F(u(s_{**}))=0$.

It remains to continue these signs to infinity.  This is precisely the
one-sided bridge argument already used in Lemma~\ref{lem:river}.  Indeed,
as long as $v<0$ and $Q_1>0$ after $s_{**}$, one has
$u'v>0$ and hence $Q_n>Q_1>0$; since $F(u)<0$ there,
\eqref{eq:B0prime} gives $B_0'>0$.  A second zero of $v$ cannot be the
first bad event, because at such a zero
\[
 Q_1=Q=r^nu'v'<0.
\]
If instead $Q_1$ vanished first while $v<0$, then
\[
 B_0=-2r^{n-1}\frac{v}{u'}E<0,
\]
contradicting $B_0>B_0(s_{**})>0$.  Hence no bad event occurs.  Thus
$\tau_{*}$ is the unique zero of $v$ on $(c_*,\infty)$ and
$Q_1>0$ on $(s_{**},\infty)$. This together with \eqref{eq:tail-prep-conclusion} yields $Q_1>0$ on $(c_{*},\infty)$.                               

Finally, $s_{**}<r_{*}$ gives $v(r_{*})<0$, while the same strict monotonicity of $B_0$ gives
$B_0(r_{*})>0$.  This proves \eqref{eq:terminal-transversality}.
head: environment

label: lem:external-hyp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:external-hyp}
Under assumption \eqref{eq:main-range}, the prescribed-node existence theorem
\cite[Theorem~1]{MTW1990} applies to \(f\).  Moreover, \(f\) satisfies the
basic assumptions $(f_1)$--$(f_2)$ of \cite{CGHY2011}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The function $f(s)=\lverts\rvert^{p-1}s-\lverts\rvert^{q-1}s$
is odd, belongs to \(C^1(\mathbb R)\), and is locally Lipschitz.  On \((0,\infty)\),
\[
 f<0\quad\hbox{on }(0,1),\qquad f(1)=0,
 \qquad
 f>0\quad\hbox{on }(1,\infty).
\]
Its primitive $F(s)$
has the unique positive zero $\beta>1$,
and \(F(s)\to\infty\) as \(\lverts\rvert\to\infty\).  Moreover,
\[
 f(s)=\lverts\rvert^{p-1}s+o(\lverts\rvert^{p})
 \quad\text{as }\lverts\rvert\to\infty,
\]
and \(1<p<(n+2)/(n-2)\).
These are the hypotheses of \cite[Theorem~1]{MTW1990}
for the present double-power nonlinearity, so for
every prescribed finite number of zeros, there is a radial solution tending
to zero at infinity.  Every finite zero is simple by ODE uniqueness.

For \cite{CGHY2011}, take \(b=1\).  The sign properties above and the zero
\(\beta\) of \(F\) give $(f_1)$.  Furthermore,
\[
 \lvertf'(s)\rvert\le p s^{p-1}+q s^{q-1}\in L^1(0,1),
\]
so $(f_2)$ also holds.
head: environment

label: lem:Wderivative
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Wderivative}
Let \(s\) be a fixed regular level on a monotone branch of the shooting
family, and                                                       
denote by $R(\alpha):=r(s,\alpha)$ the corresponding inverse radius. Then
\[
 u(R(\alpha),\alpha)=s,
 \qquad
 u'(R(\alpha),\alpha)\neq0.
\]
Moreover, \(R\) is \(C^1\) and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ralpha}
 R'(\alpha)
 =-\frac{v(R(\alpha),\alpha)}
        {u'(R(\alpha),\alpha)}.
\end{equation}
Set
\[
 D(s,\alpha)
 :=u'(R(\alpha),\alpha)^2+2F(s)
 =2E(R(\alpha),\alpha).
\]
Then the quantity
\[
 W(s,\alpha)
 :=R(\alpha)\sqrt{D(s,\alpha)}\quad \text{if }D(s,\alpha)>0
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Walpha}
 \partial_\alpha W(s,\alpha)
 =
 \frac{B_0(R(\alpha),\alpha)}
 {R(\alpha)^{n-1}\sqrt{D(s,\alpha)}}.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \(s\) is a regular value on the chosen branch,
\(u'(R(\alpha),\alpha)\neq0\).  The implicit function theorem, together
with the \(C^1\)-dependence of the shooting solution on \(\alpha\), shows
that \(R(\alpha)\) is \(C^1\).  Differentiating $u(R(\alpha),\alpha)=s$
with respect to \(\alpha\) gives
\[
 u'(R(\alpha),\alpha)R'(\alpha)
 +v(R(\alpha),\alpha)=0,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:Ralpha}.

We next differentiate \(W\) with \(s\) fixed.  To simplify the notation,
in the remainder of the proof all quantities \(u,u',u'',v,v'\) are
evaluated at \((R(\alpha),\alpha)\), and we write \(R=R(\alpha)\) and
\(D=D(s,\alpha)\).  Then                                                  
\[
 \partial_\alpha u'
 =v'+u''R'
 =v'-u''\frac{v}{u'}.
\]
Since \(F(s)\) is independent of \(\alpha\),
\[
 \partial_\alpha D
 =2u'\left(
 v'-u''\frac{v}{u'}
 \right).
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
 \sqrt D\partial_\alpha W
 =
 R'D+\frac{R}{2}\partial_\alpha D
 =
 -\frac{v}{u'}D
 +R\left(u'v'-u''v\right).
\end{align*}
Using
\[
 u''
 =-\frac{n-1}{R}u'-f(u),
 \qquad
 u=s,
\]
we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \sqrt D\partial_\alpha W
 =&
 -\frac{v}{u'}\bigl(u'^2+2F(u)\bigr)
 +R u'v'+(n-1)u'v+R f(u)v
 \\=&
 R\bigl(u'v'+f(u)v\bigr)
 +(n-2)u'v
 -2F(u)\frac{v}{u'}\\
 =&\frac{1}{R^{n-1}}
 \left(
 Q-2F(u)\frac{R^{n-1}v}{u'}
 \right)=\frac{B_0(R,\alpha)}{R^{n-1}},
\end{align*}
and \eqref{eq:Walpha} follows.
head: environment

label: lem:terminal-separation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:terminal-separation}
Let $m\ge2$ and $\alpha_*\in\mathcal G_m$.
Let $\alpha_1<\alpha_2$ be sufficiently close to
$\alpha_*$, with
$\alpha_j\in\mathcal N_{m-1}
\setminus\widetilde{\mathcal F}_m$,
$j=1,2$.
Put
\[
 w_j(r):=(-1)^{m-1} u(r,\alpha_j)
\]
on the terminal branch following \(C_{m-1}(\alpha_j)\).  Then
\(w_j>0\) and \(w_j'<0\).  Let \(r_j=r_j(s)\) be the inverse of this
branch and set
\[
 y_j(s):=-w_j'(r_j(s))>0,
 \qquad
 D_j(s):=y_j(s)^2+2F(s),
 \qquad
 W_j(s):=r_j(s)\sqrt{D_j(s)}\quad \text{if }D_j(s)>0.
\]
Let
\[
 L_j:=\lim_{r\uparrow Z_m(\alpha_j)}w_j(r).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lj-beta}
L_j=
\begin{cases}
0,
\qquad& \alpha_j\in\mathcal G_m\cup\mathcal N_m,\\
\in(0,1),
\qquad& \alpha_j\in\mathcal F_m,\quad Z_m(\alpha_j)<\infty,\\
1,
\qquad& \alpha_j\in\mathcal F_m,\quad Z_m(\alpha_j)=\infty.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Suppose that there exists $U\in (\max\{L_1,L_2\},\beta)$ such that                            
$D_j(U)>0$,
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:terminal-initial-order}
 r_1(U)\ge r_2(U),
 \qquad
 W_1(U)<W_2(U).
\end{equation}
Define
\[
 S_j:=\inf\{s\in(L_j,U]:D_j(s)>0\}.
\]
Then $S_1\ge S_2\geq 0$,
and for every \(s\in(S_1,U)\),
\begin{equation*}                               
 r_1(s)>r_2(s),
 \qquad
 W_1(s)<W_2(s),
 \qquad
 y_1(s)<y_2(s).
\end{equation*}
Moreover,
\begin{equation*}                          
 W_1(s)-W_2(s)
 \le W_1(U)-W_2(U)<0,
 \qquad s\in(S_1,U],
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}                              
 S_j=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \alpha_j\in\mathcal G_m\cup\mathcal N_m .
\end{equation*}
head: environment

label: add6.31
title: Proof
body_md:
For $L_j$, if
\(\alpha_j\in\mathcal G_m\cup\mathcal N_m\), the definitions of these
sets immediately give $L_j=0$. Suppose next that \(\alpha_j\in\mathcal F_m\) and
\(Z_m(\alpha_j)<\infty\).  By the definition of \(\mathcal F_m\), $L_j>0$.
Since \(Z_m(\alpha_j)\) is the maximal right endpoint on which $w_j>0$, $w_j'<0$,
and \(w_j(Z_m(\alpha_j))=L_j>0\), we must have $w_j'(Z_m(\alpha_j))=0$.  Moreover, $w_j''(Z_m(\alpha_j))>0$.
As \(f\) is odd, \(w_j\) satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{add6.31}
w_j''+\frac{n-1}{r}w_j'+f(w_j)=0.
\end{equation}
Evaluating \eqref{add6.31} at \(r=Z_m(\alpha_j)\) therefore yields $0<
w_j''(Z_m(\alpha_j))=-f(L_j)$,
and hence $L_j\in (0,1)$.
It remains to consider
\(\alpha_j\in\mathcal F_m\) with \(Z_m(\alpha_j)=\infty\).
In this case,
\begin{equation*}
w_j(r)\rightarrow L_j>0\quad \text{as } r\to\infty.
\end{equation*}
Set
\[
E_j(r):=\frac12 w_j'(r)^2+F(w_j(r)).
\]
Since \(w_j\) satisfies the same radial equation as \(u\), $E_j'=-\frac{n-1}{r}w_j'^2\le0$.
As \(F\) is bounded from below, \(E_j(r)\) has a finite limit as
\(r\to\infty\).  Since \(w_j\to L_j\), it follows      
that \(w_j'^2\) also has a finite limit.  This limit must be zero;
otherwise there would exist \(c>0\) and \(R>0\) such that $-w_j'(r)\ge c$ for every $r\ge R$,
which is incompatible with the convergence of \(w_j\) to the finite
limit \(L_j\).  Hence
\[
w_j'(r)\rightarrow0
\quad\text{as }r\to\infty.
\]
Using again the equation \eqref{add6.31},
we obtain
\[
w_j''(r)\rightarrow-f(L_j)\quad\text{as }r\to\infty.
\]
If \(f(L_j)\ne0\), then \(w_j''\) is eventually bounded away from zero
and has a fixed sign, which contradicts
\(w_j'\to0\).  Thus $f(L_j)=0$.
Since \(L_j>0\), we conclude
that $L_j=1$. This proves \eqref{eq:Lj-beta}.

Since \(w_j\) satisfies \eqref{add6.31}, on each inverse branch,
\begin{equation*}                                   
  r_j'(s)=-\frac1{y_j(s)},
 \qquad
 y_j'(s)=\frac{n-1}{r_j(s)}-\frac{f(s)}{y_j(s)}.
\end{equation*}
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:terminal-Dprime}
 D_j'(s)=\frac{2(n-1)y_j(s)}{r_j(s)}>0,
\end{equation}
and
\[
 W_j'(s)=H_s(y_j(s)),
 \qquad H_s(y):=
 -\frac{\sqrt{y^2+2F(s)}}{y}
 +(n-1)\frac{y}{\sqrt{y^2+2F(s)}}.
\]
For $y^2+2F(s)>0$, since  \(F(s)<0\) for \(s\in(0,\beta)\),           
\begin{equation*}                               
  \partial_y H_s(y)
 =
 \frac{2F(s)}
 {y^2\sqrt{y^2+2F(s)}}
 +
 \frac{2(n-1)F(s)}
 {(y^2+2F(s))^{\frac{3}{2}}}
 <0.
\end{equation*}


The functional $W$ is the inverse-branch quantity used in
\cite[Lemma~4.3]{CGHY2011}. For completeness, we give
a direct proof of the separation result needed here,
valid for every $n\ge3$.

By \eqref{eq:terminal-Dprime}, $D_j$ is strictly increasing
on $(L_j,U]$. If
$\alpha_j\in\mathcal G_m\cup\mathcal N_m$, then $L_j=0$ and
\[
\lim_{s\downarrow0}D_j(s)=
\begin{cases}
0, \qquad& \alpha_j\in\mathcal G_m,\\
u'(Z_m(\alpha_j),\alpha_j)^2>0,
   \qquad& \alpha_j\in\mathcal N_m.
\end{cases}
\]
The first limit follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:terminal-tail}.
Hence $D_j(s)>0$ for $s\in(0,U]$, and $S_j=0$.
If $\alpha_j\in\mathcal F_m$, then $L_j\in (0,\beta)$
and
\[
\lim_{s\downarrow L_j}D_j(s)=2F(L_j)<0.
\]
Thus $D_j$ has a unique zero $S_j\in(L_j,U)$. This proves the asserted characterization of \(S_j\).
              
   
      
                              
                                         
   
                                                  
                                                 

The initial ordering \eqref{eq:terminal-initial-order}
gives
\[
\frac{W_1(U)}{r_1(U)}
<
\frac{W_2(U)}{r_2(U)},
\]
and hence $D_1(U)<D_2(U)$ and $y_1(U)<y_2(U)$.
More generally, whenever $r_1\ge r_2$ and
$W_1<W_2$ on the common positivity interval, we have
$D_1<D_2$ and $y_1<y_2$. Therefore,
\[
(r_1-r_2)'=-\frac1{y_1}+\frac1{y_2}<0,
\qquad
(W_1-W_2)'=H_s(y_1)-H_s(y_2)>0,
\]
where the second inequality follows from
$\partial_yH_s<0$. Integrating backward from $U$, we find that,
as long as the above orderings hold,
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_1(s)-r_2(s)
=r_1(U)-r_2(U)
  -\int_s^U(r_1-r_2)'(t)\,\,\mathrm d t>r_1(U)-r_2(U)\ge0,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_1(s)-W_2(s)
=W_1(U)-W_2(U)
  -\int_s^U(W_1-W_2)'(t)\,\,\mathrm d t<W_1(U)-W_2(U)<0.
\end{aligned}
\]
These inequalities rule out any first contact
as $s$ decreases from $U$.
Consequently,
\[
r_1(s)>r_2(s),\qquad
W_1(s)<W_2(s),\qquad
y_1(s)<y_2(s)
\]
throughout the common positivity interval
$(\max\{S_1,S_2\},U)$.



                                          
                                  
   
                     
                     
              
   
                                             
   
              
                     
   

It remains to compare the lower endpoints.
Suppose that $S_1<S_2$. Then $S_2>0$ and $D_2(S_2)=0$, hence $\alpha_2\in\mathcal F_m$. By the preceding characterization, $S_2\in(L_2,U)$.
    
                                    
Since $r_2(S_2)<\infty$, we have $\lim_{s\downarrow S_2}W_2(s)=0$.
   
  
   
On the other hand, $D_1(S_2)>0$ and
$r_1(S_2)<\infty$, so $W_1(S_2)>0$.
This contradicts $W_1<W_2$ on $(S_2,U)$.
Thus $S_1\ge S_2$.
head: environment

label: prop:key
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:key}
Let \(k\ge1\) and \(\alpha_*\) be the shooting height
of a \(k\)-node bound state to \eqref{eq:shoot}.  Then there
exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
 (\alpha_* -\delta,\alpha_*)\subset\mathcal P_{k+1},
 \qquad
 {(\alpha_*,\alpha_*+\delta)
 \subset\mathcal N_{k+1}.}
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put \(m:=k+1\), then
\(\alpha_*\in\mathcal G_m\). Lemma~\ref{lem:external-hyp} and
\cite[Proposition~2.3]{CGHY2011} imply, after shrinking \(\delta>0\), that
\[
 (\alpha_*-\delta,\alpha_*+\delta)
 \subset \mathcal N_{m-1}\setminus\widetilde{\mathcal F}_m .
\]
Thus the terminal branch persists for all such \(\alpha\).

Set
\[
 w(r,\alpha):=(-1)^k u(r,\alpha),\qquad
 \psi(r,\alpha):=(-1)^k v(r,\alpha).
\]
Then \(w>0\) and \(w'<0\).                                                           
For the reference profile, the level \(w=1\) is regular.  Hence, after
reducing \(\delta\) if necessary, the implicit function theorem gives a
nearby continuation \(R(\alpha)\) such that
\[
 w(R(\alpha),\alpha)=1,
 \qquad
 w'(R(\alpha),\alpha)<0.
\]
For any
\(r_0\in(R(\alpha),Z_m(\alpha))\), we have
\[
 \lim_{r\uparrow Z_m(\alpha)}w(r,\alpha)
 \le w(r_0,\alpha)
 <w(R(\alpha),\alpha)=1.
\]
At $\alpha=\alpha_*$, Proposition~\ref{prop:tail-v} and the
simultaneous reflection $(u,v)\mapsto(w,\psi)$ give $\psi(R(\alpha_*),\alpha_*)<0$ and $B_0(R(\alpha_*),\alpha_*)>0$.
Since $R(\alpha)$,
$\psi(R(\alpha),\alpha)$ depend continuously on $\alpha$,
and $B_0$ is continuous where the radial derivative does not vanish,
these strict inequalities persist for $\alpha$ in a sufficiently
small neighborhood of $\alpha_*$.  Thus
\[
 \psi(R(\alpha),\alpha)<0,
 \qquad B_0(R(\alpha),\alpha)>0.
\]
Since
\[
 w'(R(\alpha),\alpha)^2+2F(1)
 =2E(R(\alpha),\alpha)>0,
\]
continuity and Lemma~\ref{lem:Wderivative} give, after reducing \(\delta\),
\[
 R'(\alpha)<0,\qquad
 \partial_\alpha W(1,\alpha)>0.
\]
Consequently, for every \(\alpha_1<\alpha_2\) sufficiently close to \(\alpha_*\),                    
\[
 r_1(1)>r_2(1),\qquad W_1(1)<W_2(1),
\]
and Lemma~\ref{lem:terminal-separation} applies with \(U=1\).

First let \(\alpha_1=\alpha_*<\alpha_2\). Since
\(\alpha_1\in\mathcal G_m\), by Lemma~\ref{lem:terminal-separation}, we have \(S_1=0\), hence                            
\(S_2=0\), and therefore $\alpha_2\in\mathcal G_m\cup\mathcal N_m$.
If \(\alpha_2\in\mathcal G_m\), both shots are decaying. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:terminal-tail}, $r_j(s)y_j(s)\to0$ as $s\rightarrow0$,
and, since \(F(s)<0\),
\[
 0<W_j(s)\le r_j(s)y_j(s)\to0.
\]
This contradicts
\[
 W_1(s)-W_2(s)
 \le W_1(1)-W_2(1)<0.
\]
Thus \(\alpha_2\in\mathcal N_m\).

Now let \(\alpha_1<\alpha_2=\alpha_*\). Then  \(\alpha_2\in\mathcal G_m\) and \(S_2=0\). If \(S_1=0\), then
\(\alpha_1\in\mathcal G_m\cup\mathcal N_m\). The case
\(\alpha_1\in\mathcal G_m\) is excluded by the same \(W\)-gap argument.
If \(\alpha_1\in\mathcal N_m\), Lemma~\ref{lem:terminal-separation} gives
\(y_1(s)<y_2(s)\) for small $s>0$, whereas
\[
 \lim_{s\downarrow0}y_1(s)
 =\lvertu'(Z_m(\alpha_1),\alpha_1)\rvert>0,
 \qquad
 \lim_{s\downarrow0}y_2(s)=\lvertu'(Z_m(\alpha_2),\alpha_2)\rvert=0,
\]
a contradiction. Hence \(S_1>0\), and therefore $\alpha_1\in\mathcal F_m\subset\mathcal P_m$. This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:ground-threshold
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ground-threshold}
Assume \eqref{eq:main-range}. Then there exists a unique $\alpha_0>1$ such that
\[
\mathcal G_1=\{\alpha_0\}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\mathcal P_1=(1,\alpha_0),
\qquad
\mathcal N_1=(\alpha_0,\infty).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Existence follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:external-hyp}, while uniqueness
follows from the Serrin--Tang criterion
\cite[Theorem~1]{SerrinTang2000}, since for $s>1$,
\[
K(s):=\frac{s f'(s)}{f(s)}
=\frac{p s^{d}-q}{s^{d}-1},
\qquad
K'(s)
=-\frac{(d)^2s^{d-1}}
       {(s^{d}-1)^2}<0.
\]
Thus $\mathcal G_1=\{\alpha_0\}$.

Since \(E(r,\alpha_0)\to0\) as \(r\to\infty\) and \(E\) is strictly decreasing, we have \(E(r,\alpha_0)>0\) for every finite \(r\).
Consequently
\(F(\alpha_0)=E(0)>0\), so \(\alpha_0>\beta\). On the other hand, for the shot with
\(\alpha=\beta\), one has  $E(0,\beta)=F(\beta)=0$.                   
Since \(E\) is decreasing,
this shot cannot reach \(u=0\), and therefore
\(\beta\in\mathcal P_1\).

By \cite[Proposition~2.2]{CGHY2011}, the sets
\(\mathcal P_1\) and \(\mathcal N_1\) are open and $(1,\infty)
 =\mathcal P_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}
  \mathcal G_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\mathcal N_1$.
Since \(\beta\in(1,\alpha_0)\cap\mathcal P_1\), connectedness yields $\mathcal P_1=(1,\alpha_0)$.
Moreover, Lemma~\ref{lem:external-hyp} provides a \(1\)-node bound state, so \(\mathcal N_1\ne\varnothing\). Connectedness then gives $\mathcal N_1=(\alpha_0,\infty)$.
head: environment

label: lem:jumping
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:jumping}
Assume that $\mathcal N_{j-1}=
\mathcal P_j\mathbin{\dot\cup}
\mathcal G_j\mathbin{\dot\cup}
\mathcal N_j$, $j\ge2$,
where $\mathcal P_j$ and $\mathcal N_j$ are relatively open in
$\mathcal N_{j-1}$.
If $\mathcal N_{j-1}=(\alpha_{j-2},\infty)$
and $\mathcal G_j\neq\varnothing$, then there exists a unique
$\alpha_{j-1}>\alpha_{j-2}$ such that
\[
\mathcal G_j=\{\alpha_{j-1}\},
\qquad
\mathcal P_j=(\alpha_{j-2},\alpha_{j-1}),
\qquad
\mathcal N_j=(\alpha_{j-1},\infty).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take $\gamma\in\mathcal G_j$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:key},
$\mathcal N_j$ contains a right neighborhood of $\gamma$.
We claim that $(\gamma,\infty)\subset\mathcal N_j$.
Otherwise, let
\[
b=\sup\{s>\gamma:(\gamma,s)\subset\mathcal N_j\}<\infty.
\]
Since $\mathcal N_j$ is relatively open, $b\notin\mathcal N_j$.
Also $b\notin\mathcal P_j$, because the openness of $\mathcal P_j$
would contradict $(\gamma,b)\subset\mathcal N_j$.
Hence $b\in\mathcal G_j$. The local shooting separation property at $b$ gives $(b-\delta,b)\subset\mathcal P_j$
for some $\delta>0$, again contradicting
$(\gamma,b)\subset\mathcal N_j$. Thus
\[
(\gamma,\infty)\subset\mathcal N_j.
\]
This immediately implies that $\gamma$ is the only point of
$\mathcal G_j$: if $\eta>\gamma$ belonged to $\mathcal G_j$, then
$\eta\in\mathcal N_j$; while if $\eta<\gamma$ belonged to
$\mathcal G_j$, applying the preceding argument to $\eta$ would give
$\gamma\in\mathcal N_j$.

Therefore
\[
\mathcal G_j=\{\gamma\}.
\]
Since
\[
(\alpha_{j-2},\gamma)
=
\bigl(\mathcal P_j\cap(\alpha_{j-2},\gamma)\bigr)
\mathbin{\dot\cup}
\bigl(\mathcal N_j\cap(\alpha_{j-2},\gamma)\bigr),
\]
and both sets are relatively open, the connectedness of
$(\alpha_{j-2},\gamma)$, together with the left-hand local shooting separation property,
yields
\[
(\alpha_{j-2},\gamma)\subset\mathcal P_j.
\]
Setting $\alpha_{j-1}=\gamma$ completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:external-hyp} gives $\mathcal G_{k+1}\neq\varnothing$
for every \(k\ge1\), since a profile in \(\mathcal G_{k+1}\) has
exactly \(k\) zeros.
For \(k\ge1\), Proposition~\ref{prop:tail-v} provides the terminal
transversality
\[
v(r_*)<0,\qquad B_0(r_*)>0.
\]
Here Proposition~\ref{prop:tail-v} relies on the finite-phase induction
summarized in Proposition~\ref{cor:variation-finite}, which in turn
follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:firstphase},
Corollary~\ref{addcor2}, and Proposition~\ref{prop:phase}.
Consequently, Proposition~\ref{prop:key} yields the local shooting separation property
at every point of \(\mathcal G_j\), \(j\ge2\).

Lemma~\ref{lem:ground-threshold} gives the initial level \(j=1\).
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:jumping} inductively, we conclude that $\mathcal G_{k+1}$
consists of exactly one shooting height for every \(k\ge1\).
Since the radial initial-value problem is uniquely determined by the
shooting height \(\alpha=u(0)>0\), there is at most one radial bound
state with exactly \(k\) nodes and positive value at the origin.
Together with the existence supplied by
Lemma~\ref{lem:external-hyp}, this proves Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:shooting-structure}
Let $\alpha_k=u_k(0)$ for $k\ge1$, and let
$\alpha_0$ denote the ground-state shooting height.
Then
\[
\beta<\alpha_0<\alpha_1<\alpha_2<\cdots.
\]
Moreover, the shooting variation
$v=\partial_\alpha u$ along the $k$-node
bound state has exactly $k+1$ simple zeros
in $(0,\infty)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The strict ordering follows from
Lemmas~\ref{lem:ground-threshold}
and~\ref{lem:jumping}.
The exact zero count follows from
Propositions~\ref{cor:variation-finite}
and \ref{prop:tail-v}.
All zeros are simple by uniqueness
for the variational equation.
